articles.title: India wants more Olympic medals but 'doesn't participate in half the sports'; PM Modi speaks out 'bitter truth'
articles.summary: Off the field News: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday said India cannot expect a significant rise in its Olympic medal tally unless it starts competing .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday said India cannot expect a significant rise in its Olympic medal tally unless it starts competing in many sports where it currently has little or no representation, including surfing and sport climbing.Addressing athletes, students and volunteers virtually during the Khelo India Dialogue ahead of National Sports Day on August 29, PM Modi said India's sports vision is not just about winning medals but also about making sports a part of nation-building.Sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya joined the event virtually from IIT Gandhinagar.Prime Minister Modi pointed out that India still does not compete in many Olympic sports. "In the Olympics, there are so many different sports... Indian teams don't even participate in half of them, which means that we are not competing for a major chunk of the medal tally," Modi said, calling it a "bitter truth".He said this has been the situation for many years."And this has been going on for decades. In 2012, we competed in only 13 sports. We were not even there in over 20 events and not many in the country even knew about some of these competitions."Other countries win medals in those sports, and we don't even participate. To increase our medals, we have to improve in these sports," he pointed out.India participated in 16 of the 32 sports at the 2024 Paris Olympics.PM Modi specifically mentioned surfing and sport climbing, two sports that are part of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics but have never seen an Indian competitor."For example surfing and sport climbing...We have such a vast coastline, we have such a vast hilly region where there could be a natural affinity for sports like these. from water sports to winter sports, we have the required demography as well as geography," he asserted.He said India has the natural conditions to develop athletes in these sports."Despite this, we are not seen in these sports anywhere in the world. That's why we have to find opportunities of growing these sports in different regions. To increase our medal tally, we will have to master these sports as well," he added.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Power Ranking Every NHL Division Heading Into the 2026-27 Season
articles.summary: Thirty-two days from now, it's a moot point.
articles.body:
Thirty-two days from now, it's a moot point.

That's the day on which pucks drop in five NHL cities to kick off the league's 2026-27 regular season, which will stretch to 84 games for the first time since 1993-94.

The defending champion Carolina Hurricanes will raise a banner that afternoon against the team that won the previous two Stanley Cups, the Florida Panthers.

The Hurricanes accrued 113 points in 2025-26 and lapped the field in the Metropolitan Division, then got even hotter in the postseason and eliminated Ottawa, Philadelphia, Montreal and Vegas—going 16-3 in the playoffs on the way to their first championship victory since 2006.

Having the champs is a huge competitive feather in the cap of the Metropolitan, but B/R's hockey team looked at the four divisions from top to bottom in assembling a preseason power ranking of the divisions as the schedule's start draws near.

Take a look at what we came up with and drop a thought in the app comments.

That's the phrase no less of an authority than Connor McDavid used when describing how his Edmonton Oilers were " fortunate " to play in the Pacific when chasing a playoff berth down the stretch in 2025-26.

Edmonton finished 14th overall in the league with 41 wins and 93 points but copped second in the Pacific, just two points off the pace of the first-place Vegas Golden Knights, who finished tied for 12th overall with a team (Washington) that didn't even qualify for the Eastern Conference playoffs.

"It's a bit of a pillow fight right now," McDavid said.

Indeed, in spite of the presence of McDavid, Leon Draisaitl, Macklin Celebrini and other talented youngsters in both San Jose and Anaheim, truer words were never spoken.

If you're looking for a top-heavy group, nobody beats the Central.

The "other" Western Conference division had the Presidents' Trophy winners from Colorado and the third-place overall team in Dallas, not to mention the No. 7 finisher in Minnesota.

Those three teams combined for 151 wins and captured nearly 68.5 percent of possible standings points, but we can't consider ourselves responsible journalists unless we look at the rest of the division—namely Utah, St. Louis, Nashville, Winnipeg and Chicago—only one of which (Utah) made the playoffs while the other four finished among the league's bottom 11 out of 32.

Maybe Nathan MacKinnon is the best player in the league. Certainly you can argue that either Quinn Hughes or Cale Makar is its best defenseman.

But put the Avalanche and Wild together with the rest of the flotsam and jetsam and the collective quickly goes downhill.

As we mentioned earlier, all the Metropolitan Division really has to do in a competition like this is pull on a Carolina Hurricanes sweater and yell, "Scoreboard!"

But let's face it, Carolina's march to the 2026 Stanley Cup was as much a product of an obscenely hot playoff run—8-0 through two rounds, 12-1 through three—as it was a dominant blitz through the regular season.

None of the other seven teams in the division got to 100 points and five of them missed the playoffs entirely. So if you want to contend that the Metropolitan belongs no better than equal to or below the Central, we'll listen.

But when it comes to hockey lists, possession of the Cup is nine-tenths of the law.

OK, we'll say it: Not only will more than one team from the Atlantic amass more than 100 points across 84 games from September to April, but we'll go a step further and say at least one Atlantic team (if not more) will hoist a Cup in the next few seasons.

And it's certainly no stretch to say it'll be next spring.

Lest anyone forget, the Atlantic had four 100-point teams and five playoff participants in its ranks last season, and that doesn't even include the injury-ravaged Panthers—who missed out on the 2025-26 postseason party after having gone the distance to win consecutive Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25.

Think they won't be back in the mix again this season? Think again.

The folks at DraftKings have already installed Florida alongside Carolina as the top pick to hoist the chalice in 2027 at +650 apiece , and two of the other top-10 picks—Tampa Bay at +1200 and Montreal at +2200—are reppin' the Atlantic, too.

articles.title: Spikes Under the Lights TV Schedule, Live Stream, Prize Money, Teams & Preview for Volleyball Event
articles.summary: College volleyball will take center stage at AT&T Stadium on Thursday night as some of the top teams in the country take part in the first-ever Spikes Under the Lights event.
articles.body:
College volleyball will take center stage at AT&T Stadium on Thursday night as some of the top teams in the country take part in the first-ever Spikes Under the Lights event.

The winner of the exhibition tournament will walk away with a big share of the event's $1 million prize pool .

Ahead of the event, here's a look at the TV schedule and a preview of each team.

Match 1: No. 1 Nebraska vs. No. 11 SMU, 8 p.m. ET, TNT Sports

Match 2: No. 10 Penn State vs. No. 17 Florida, 9 p.m. ET, TNT Sports

Final: winner of Match 1 vs. winner of Match 2, 10 p.m. ET, TNT Sports

Even to those unfamiliar with college volleyball, Nebraska is a name that carries plenty of weight in the sport. The Cornhuskers have won five NCAA tournaments, with the most recent one coming in 2017.

This year's team figures to bring Nebraska back to the national stage after a few years away from its last championship game appearance. The veteran group of Andi Jackson, Harper Murray and Bergen Reilly will lead the way for the Cornhuskers.

Much like Nebraska, Penn State has dominated the sport across several decades and is just two seasons removed from its last national title.

The Nittany Lions faced a second-round exit last year but have a promising duo of Kennedy Martin and setter Alexis Stuckey to guide them this year.

SMU doesn't have the history of a Nebraska or Penn State, but the Mustangs are perhaps on their way to forming a dynasty.

SMU finished 26-7 in Sam Erger's second season in 2023 and went 25-8 last year, reaching the second round of the NCAA tournament for a second consecutive season.

The Mustangs bring back a handful of key veterans as well as an exciting new outside hitter in Suli Davis.

The Gators entered a new era under Ryan Theis last year after Mary Wise coached the team for more than 30 years. Naturally, there were some growing pains as Florida finished 16-12, but the Gators figure to be in for a much better 2026.

Theis lost a handful of star power from last season but still has a roster anchored by Alec Rothe and Jordan Byrd.

articles.summary: Hockey News: India ended their Women’s Hockey World Cup campaign on a high, beating Germany 3-1 in the fifth-sixth place classification match to secure their best-.
articles.body: India ended their Women’s Hockey World Cup campaign on a high, beating Germany 3-1 in the fifth-sixth place classification match to secure their best-ever finish at the tournament in 52 years.The contest at Wagener Hockey Stadium was tightly fought in the opening half, with neither team able to find the breakthrough. Germany had the better share of penalty-corner opportunities, but their execution lacked precision.India’s best spell came in the second quarter when Navneet Kaur and Salima Tete combined to test German goalkeeper Finja Starck three times, only to be denied each time.India turn the game around after the breakThe match changed dramatically in the third quarter. India finally broke the deadlock in the 43rd minute when Ishika was played through and produced a composed reverse-lift that beat Starck.Navneet then doubled India’s advantage a minute later. After winning another penalty corner, she used a touch-and-slap finish to send the ball into the net. Three minutes later, she struck again, showing excellent composure to dribble past the goalkeeper before calmly lifting the ball over her.India entered the final quarter with a commanding 3-0 lead and defended it with discipline. Savita made two important saves in the closing stages, but Germany eventually pulled one back in the 59th minute when Krings converted a rebound.Germany earned another penalty corner with only seconds remaining, but it was too late to change the result.India held on for a 3-1 victory, securing fifth place and completing a memorable campaign. articles.title: Dos Santos y Russell revolucionan las vallas mundiales con dos récords antológicos
articles.standfirst: El brasileño firma en Zúrich un impresionante registro de 45.80, superando la plusmarca de Warholm, mientras que la estadounidense corre en 12.09 los 100 vallas femeninos
articles.summary: El brasileño establece un impresionante registro de 45.80, superando el tiempo que el noruego, que corría en la calle anexa, firmó en 2021 con 45.94
articles.body: Revolución en las vallas mundiales con dos nombres propios: Alison Dos Santos y Masai Russell. Ambos aprovecharon la gran jornada en la pista de Zúrich para causar un terremoto en los rankings universales de 400 y 100 metros vallas respectivamente. El primero fue el de Alison Dos Santos, que ya había dado muestras en Silesia de su gran estado de forma en los 400 metros vallas. Allí, el brasileño batió a Karsten Warholm, plusmarquista mundial de la distancia, que sólo unos días más tarde ha dejado de serlo. En una impresionante prueba en Zúrich, la última reunión de Liga de Diamante antes de las finales del circuito (que se disputan en septiembre), Dos Santos corrió para la historia. Con una gran salida de tacos, se situó primero antes de la curva, superando prácticamente al noruego, al que le gusta correr siempre por la calle 7 y que asistía atónito a la carrera de su rival. Faltaba por ver si en el tramo final de carrera, Dos Santos podría aguantar el ritmo sin desfallecer. Pero lo hizo. Superó con facilidad las dos últimas vallas para alcanzar la meta en un estratosférico 45.80, con el que estableció un nuevo récord mundial. Esta vez, Warholm, que felicitó a su rival tal y como cruzó la meta, fue segundo, con 46.69. Seis años después de que el noruego estableciera en los Juegos Olímpicos de Tokio ese registro, con 45.94, cede la plusmarca a Dos Santos, que mejoró con creces su registro personal (46.29). En la prueba corta de vallas femenina, la gran protagonista fue Masai Russell, que realizó una soberbia carrera para establecer un nuevo récord del mundo. La estadounidense, que se había mostrado muy solvente toda la temporada, corrió en 12.09 con viento cero (0.0) para rebajar en 0.03 segundos la plusmarca universal que la nigeriana Tobi Amusan firmó en 2022. Precisamente Amusan fue segunda, con 12.23, mientras que tercera fue la neerlandesa Nadine Visser, con 12.34. Armand Duplantis sumó este jueves otra victoria en Liga de Diamante en el mejor concurso de pértiga de la historia. El sueco estuvo a punto de batir la plusmarca mundial en 6,32, pero firmó el récord del mitin, con 6,25, y con su principal rival, Karalis, también por encima de 6,20, récord nacional de Grecia. 'Mondo', algo irregular esta temporada, arrancó en 5,65, que superó a la primera, para renunciar después a 5,80. El sueco saltó de nuevo a la primera 5,90, y volvió a descansar sobre 6,00, altura que sí firmó Karalis y que permitió al griego situarse líder del concurso de forma provisional. Porque Karalis se ha erigido en un competidor brutal, un rival que empieza a acechar al plusmaquista mundial. Así lo hizo también en Zúrich. El griego, consciente de que tiene que mejorar a golpe de récord nacional para rivalizar con 'Mondo', sigue creciendo. Después de saltar 6,10, renunció a los 6,15 y pidió el listón en 6,20. Unos minutos antes, Duplantis sí había saltado 6,15 para establecer el récord del mitin. Pero 'Manolo' quería más y saltó con éxito en su primer intento sobre 6,20, nuevo récord nacional y también plusmarca del mitin. Duplantis respondió en esta particular partida de ajedrez entre ambos y saltó a la primera 6,25, de nuevo registro del mitin. Así que el griego respondió pidiendo el listón en 6,32, altura que suponía récord del mundo. Firmó tres nulos, para dejar vía libre al mejor pertiguista de la historia. El sueco lo intentó y estuvo a punto de sobrepasar la altura en su tercera tentativa, pero se tuvo que 'conformar' con otra victoria y récord del mitin. La suiza Audrey Werro sigue acechando el récord que Jarmila Kratochvilova firmó en los 800 metros en 1983, el más antiguo que pervive en el atletismo (1:53.28). La reciente campeona de Europa de la distancia firmó una magistral carrera, en la que Femke Bol demostró de nuevo que su paso a la distancia desde los 400 metros vallas es un éxito, para sellar la tercera mejor marca de la historia, con 1:53.70. Sin Hodgkinson en liza por lesión, las dos favoritas se fueron tras la liebre, que tenía el requerimiento de pasar los 400 metros en 55.50. Bol, que estuvo a punto de superar a su rival en meta hace unos días en Silesia, se colocó primera con el objetivo de tener ciera ventaja. Pasaron en 55.36 al toque de campana pero Werro, que controla la distancia a su antojo, aún no había dicho su última palabra. La suiza respondió con un cambio en la contrarrecta para colocarse primera y alcanzar la meta en 1:53.70. Es la única atleta que ha bajado tres veces de los 1:54.00. Bol finalizó segunda, con otro récord nacional (1:54.71). En los 800 metros masculinos, el triunfo fue para el keniata Wanyonyi, con 1:41.76, líder mundial del año, por delante de Sedjati (1:41.83). Mo Attaoui se retiró antes de terminar la carrera. Por su parte, en longitud, Tentoglou se llevó la victoria, con 8,45, en un concurso en el que Lester Lescay fue octavo, con 7,85. En una de las mejores carreras de 100 metros de la temporada, Julien Alfred y Melissa Jefferson-Wooden firmaron un duelo magistral. Con gran diferencia sobre sus rivales, la primera la estadounidense Sha'Carri Richardson (10.97) que acabó tercera, la campeona olímpica superó por cinco milésimas a la campeona del mundo. Ambas firmaron un registro de 10.70, con viento en contra (-0.7 m/s), que supone récord nacional de Alfred, mientras que la estadounidense firmó su mejor registro de la temporada. Antes de las pruebas que puntuaban para el Circuito del Diamante, se disputaron varias pruebas con participación española. En el 1.500 femenino, Marta García, subcampeona de Europa de 5.000, fue tercera, con 4:03.86, su mejor registro de la temporada en la distancia, en una carrera que se llevó la italiana Cavalli, con 4:03.27. Por su parte, en los 200 metros, Jael Bestué también firmó la tercera posición, con 22.74, por detrás de la suiza Hoenke (22.53) y la australiana Lewis (22.66). Además, en los 110 metros vallas, en la victoria del suizo Joseph (13.11), Quique Llopis terminó cuarto, con 13.35, mientras que Asier Martínez alcanzó la meta en octava posición (13.49).

articles.title: Diamond League results: Audrey Werro comes up just short in 800m world record bid
articles.summary: European champion Audrey Werro came tantalisingly close to downing the oldest outdoor world record in athletics, finishing a little more than four tenths of a second off Jarmila Kratochvilova's 800m mark.
articles.body:
European champion Audrey Werro came tantalisingly close to downing the oldest outdoor world record in athletics, finishing a little more than four tenths of a second off Jarmila Kratochvilova's 800m mark of one minute 53.28 seconds, set 43 years ago.

Roared on by a 25,000-strong capacity crowd at the Zurich Diamond League, the Swiss hit the final 100m almost in stride with the infield pacing lights which had been set for a world record.

However Werro, straining hard against the clock, could not quite find the finishing pace she needed, clocking 1:53.70.

Still, the third-fastest time in history shaves another tenth of a second off the 22-year-old's personal best and only increases the sense that she will break the record sooner rather than later.

Werro has improved every year of her top-level career and now, having finished her studies and concentrating on the track, has shown ruthless consistency. She has four of the top-10 all-time 800m times, all clocked this summer.

For Britain's Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson, who withdrew from the meeting after her exertions in taking continental silver behind Werro in Birmingham, it only emphasised the challenge she faces in the event.

Not only does she have to contend with Werro's burgeoning form, but Femke Broeders-Bol, the world 400m hurdles champion who has switched up to two laps this season, gave another impressive showing in her debut campaign over 800m.

The Dutchwoman, who took out the pace initially, clocked a new national record of 1:54.71, beating Hodgkinson's training partner and Commonwealth 800m champion Georgia Hunter Bell into third.

When Athing Mu-Nikolayev, Hodgkinson's American nemesis who beat her to gold at Tokyo 2021 and Eugene 2022, slipped off the scene, the Briton had hoped to dominate the 800m.

With less than two years until she defends her Olympic crown in Los Angeles however, new rivals are looking ever more threatening.

While Werro fell short in her world record attempt, two new marks were set in an astonishng night of action.

First, Brazil's Alison dos Santos defied expectations to smash the 400m hurdles world record.

The 26-year-old has been in excellent form this season, undefeated in the event, but there was little to suggest that Karsten Warholm's 2021 mark of 45.94 seconds was in danger.

But, with Warholm a distant second, Tokyo 2025 silver medallist Dos Santos cantered off the final hurdle and pushed through to clock 45.80 seconds.

His previous personal best stood at 46.29 and was set four years ago.

Just 75 minutes later, another world record fell in front of the 25,000-strong capacity crowd

Masai Russell, the Olympic champion, capturing the 100m hurdles mark was less surprising, considering the American has finished within a tenth of a second of Tobi Amusan's 12.12-second landmark five times in the past two seasons.

The 26-year-old celebrated her 12.09 clocking with a finger to her lips as the crowd erupted. Just like Warholm, Amusan had a prime view of her record being broken, finishing second.

Amy Hunt, winner of four golds at the European Championships earlier this month, found things tougher against some of the world's finest 100m runners.

Left in the blocks, the Briton had to watch on as Olympic champion Julian Alfred inflicted Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's first defeat over the distance in two years, edging out the American in a photo finish.

David Rudisha's 800m world record of one minute 40.91 seconds, set en route to gold at London 2012, survived unscathed as his Kenyan compatriot Emmanuel Wanyonyi came home in one minute 41.76 seconds.

While Sweden's Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis, pushed on by competition from Greece's Emmanouil Karalis, failed in three shots at improving his own pole vault world record to 6.32m.

articles.title: Spikes Under the Lights Winner, Prize Money and Top Highlights from Volleyball Event
articles.summary: The first-ever Spikes Under the Lights event took place at AT&T Stadium in Dallas as four of college volleyball's top teams battled for the chance at a $150,000 prize.
articles.body:
The first-ever Spikes Under the Lights event took place at AT&T Stadium in Dallas as four of college volleyball's top teams battled for the chance at a $150,000 prize.

No. 1 Nebraska, No. 10 Penn State, No. 11 SMU and No. 17 Florida each received $200,000 for participating in the event, but only one team could walk away with an additional $150,000.

Nebraska and Florida were up first, and the top-ranked Cornhuskers got out to a strong start as they won the first set 21-19 after an exciting rally on set point.

College volleyball tournament has $1M prize pool

The second set was highly competitive, but Nebraska walked away with the win after a monster serve to send the Huskers to the finals. Nebraska finished the match with 23 kills, 26 digs, a pair of aces and seven blocks.

SMU and Penn State squared off in the other semifinal game, and the Mustangs picked up a win in the first set after plenty of back and forth with the Nittany Lions.

The Mustangs then took the second set to advance to the championship match after Suli Davis, who finished with 11 kills, delivered a game-winning spike.

The Mustangs are a team on the rise in college volleyball, and picking up a win over a top-10 team was the perfect way to start the season.

articles.title: After historic World Cup finish, Savita Punia urges PM Modi to ‘Save WHIL’
articles.summary: Hockey News: Kolkata: India’s best World Cup finish in 52 years prompted an appeal from former India captain and goalkeeper Savita Punia, who wrote to Prime Minist.
articles.body: Kolkata: India’s best World Cup finish in 52 years prompted an appeal from former India captain and goalkeeper Savita Punia, who wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi on social media after the team’s historic campaign — asking him to help save the Women’s Hockey India League (WHIL).Hours after India finished fifth at the World Cup in Amstelveen on Thursday, Savita posted a series of messages on ‘X’, tagging the Prime Minister, union sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya, several other ministers, Odisha chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi, sporting personalities and potential corporate backers.“Sir, our women just rewrote hockey history after 52 years. The league that built these players — the Women’s HIL — needs support to survive. A word from you could change its fate,” she wrote while tagging Modi.The timing of the appeal was significant. India had just completed one of their finest World Cup campaigns, beating world No. 5 Germany 3-1 to finish fifth — their best result since the inaugural World Cup in 1974, when they finished fourth.But while the result offered plenty to celebrate, Savita’s posts highlighted a concern away from the pitch — the uncertain future of WHIL. Savita believes the league is too important to allow it to disappear.“The WHIL is that platform. It creates opportunities, develops talent and builds the pipeline for future World Cup & Olympic stars,” she wrote in another post, before making a direct appeal to govt ministers: “Let’s ensure the girls coming through today have a league to dream of playing in tomorrow.”The India captain also reached out to some of the country’s biggest sporting and entertainment names, asking them to use their influence to bring visibility and potential sponsors to women’s hockey.Tagging Shah Rukh Khan, Priyanka Chopra and Ananya Birla, she wrote: “Women’s hockey needs your voice right now. A single tweet from you could bring sponsors and visibility back to WHIL.”She also appealed to Reliance Foundation and Nita Ambani, pointing to their work in grassroots sport and Olympic talent development. “Women’s HIL is exactly the kind of grassroots-to-elite pipeline that needs a backer like this right now,” she wrote.Savita did not forget those who have already supported the women’s game. She thanked Parth Jindal and JSW, along with the Delhi Pipers and Bengal Tigers ownership groups, for standing behind women’s hockey and urged others to follow their example.The message running through her posts was stark: the success India enjoyed in Netherlands cannot be taken for granted.“The math is simple: no league → no talent pool → no next generation → no World Cup medal,” Savita wrote. “Our women got India’s best finish in 52 years WITH a struggling league. Imagine what’s possible if we actually invest in it.”For a team that has just shown it can compete with the world’s best, Savita’s appeal is ultimately about making sure the next generation gets the same opportunity — and that the pathway to the national team does not disappear just when Indian women’s hockey appears to be moving forward.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Neeraj Chopra qualifies for Diamond League Finals despite competing in just two events; here's how
articles.summary: More sports News: India's javelin thrower Neeraj Chopra has qualified for the Diamond League Finals in Brussels on September 5, even though he competed in only two Diam.
articles.body: India's javelin thrower Neeraj Chopra has qualified for the Diamond League Finals in Brussels on September 5, even though he competed in only two Diamond League meetings this season.The final standings were updated after the last Diamond League meeting in Zurich on Thursday. Chopra finished sixth in the standings with 12 points after securing second place in Doha on June 19 and Lausanne on August 21.The top six athletes in the men's javelin standings qualify for the Diamond League Finals.This season had 14 Diamond League meetings, but men's javelin was part of only five of them. Chopra competed in just two because he was recovering from a lower back injury that has troubled him since September last year.The injury delayed his return until the Diamond League meeting in Doha.Chopra was not fully fit at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, where he won the silver medal with a season-best throw of 85.83 metres. He later improved that mark to 88.05 metres at the Lausanne Diamond League.The Diamond League Finals will be held over two days in Brussels on September 4 and 5. The men's javelin final is scheduled for September 5.The winner of each event will receive a trophy and at least USD 30,000 in prize money, while the eighth-place finisher will receive USD 1,000. articles.body: NEW DELHI: India women’s hockey team chief coach Sjoerd Marijne has defended his decision to take leave shortly before the FIH World Cup, insisting his absence did not compromise the team’s preparations and that he remained closely involved in the build-up to the tournament.Marijne’s decision to take leave before the World Cup had come under scrutiny in a section of the media, with legendary former India goalkeeper PR Sreejesh questioning whether a team could perform at its best when its chief coach was away during the final phase of preparation.India eventually finished fifth at the World Cup, putting together a creditable campaign after entering the tournament with several challenges, including injuries.Marijne, however, said his leave did not mean he was disconnected from the team or unaware of what was happening during the preparation period.“I have seen every training, match, done meetings and had personal contact with the players, so it was not that I didn't know what was going on,” Marijne told PTI in an interview after India's World Cup campaign.“People don't always know the real story and that's fine as long as we know what we have done and we covered everything. Besides this also the staff which was there and helped them to prepare for the World Cup,” he said.Marijne wants India to keep raising the barMarijne, who returned for his second stint as India’s coach in January, said the fifth-place finish should not become the ceiling for the team. Instead, he wants the players to retain the hunger that helped them transform from an injury-hit side into a competitive World Cup unit.“It has been a journey with many ups and this is what we have to continue, but that's only possible when we stay hungry and eager to get the best out of ourselves and not take things easy.“Keep raising the bar, and expect more and more from the team. Growing is a daily process and also staying connected with each other,” he said.The Dutchman said his second stint began differently from his first spell because the current group already had experience of playing against higher-ranked teams and competing at major tournaments.“This is a team which has players who already had played against high-ranked teams and experienced to play big tournaments. In the beginning we didn't have this and these girls also knew me, how I coach and prepare the team. They already had shared this with the younger girls. This made it easier to have a quick start,” he said.From ‘I’ to ‘we’: Marijne’s focus on team identityMarijne identified rebuilding the team’s collective identity as his immediate priority after returning to the setup.“The main challenge was to make again a team and change the mindset to 'we' instead of 'I' and bring back discipline,” he said.He also believes he returned to India as a more mature coach after spending the intervening years working with and guiding other coaches.“I have been in India, I know better how things are working and what works with coaching an Indian team. I have guided coaches the last years and that also helped me to reflect myself and become a better coach,” he said.The coach hopes the team’s World Cup performance can also generate greater interest in women’s hockey in India.“If I see the reactions, people are positive and follow the team. I hope we inspire young kids to also start playing hockey,” he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: The Diamond League saw two world records in hurdles broken by Masai Russell and Alison dos Santos.
articles.body:
The Diamond League saw two world records in hurdles broken by Masai Russell and Alison dos Santos.

Russell is the new world-record holder in the women's 100-meter hurdles after clocking an official time of 12.09 seconds.

Dos Santos set the new mark in the men's 400-meter hurdles with a time of 45.80 seconds.

"I felt like [I could break the world record] throughout the whole season. Today I was able to execute," dos Santos said after his historic run.

The previous women's 100-meter hurdles record of 12.12 seconds by Tobi Amusan stood for more than four years.

Norway's Karsten Warholm held the men's 400-meter hurdles record since 2021 when he broke it twice. He originally set the mark of 46.70 seconds at the Diamond League, then followed it up with a run of 45.94 seconds at the Tokyo Olympics.

articles.title: From Anaya Bangar’s cricket return to Imane Khelif’s Olympic gold controversy: The biggest transgender and gender-eligibility debates in sport
articles.summary: More sports News: NEW DELHI: Anaya Bangar's return to cricket has opened a much bigger conversation about transgender athletes in sport, one that now extends far beyond.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Anaya Bangar's return to cricket has opened a much bigger conversation about transgender athletes in sport, one that now extends far beyond the cricket field.The former Mumbai Under-19 cricketer has received clearance from Cricket Australia to play women's community cricket in the country, giving her a route back into competitive cricket after beginning her transition in 2022. Bangar can participate in Premier Cricket, which Cricket Australia classifies as community cricket, immediately. Her pathway to elite cricket from March 2027, however, comes with eligibility conditions, including a requirement to provide a blood test confirming that her serum testosterone remains below the prescribed threshold and that she continues to meet the governing body's policy requirements.The decision has already divided opinion. South Africa all-rounder Marizanne Kapp publicly criticised Cricket Australia's position, describing the decision as "absolutely ridiculous" and arguing against transgender women competing in women's cricket.Bangar's case is therefore not simply about one cricketer. The Olympics have taken a very different routeLaurel Hubbard: the Olympic milestoneFew athletes illustrate that change more clearly than New Zealand weightlifter Laurel Hubbard.Hubbard became the first openly transgender woman to compete at an Olympic Games when she took part in the women's super-heavyweight weightlifting competition at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. She did not complete a successful lift in the competition and finished without a result. At the time, her participation was viewed as a landmark moment for transgender representation in elite sport.Five years later, the IOC has adopted a fundamentally different approach. From Los Angeles 2028, transgender women who do not satisfy the IOC's biological-sex eligibility requirements will not be eligible for the women's category at the Games.Lia Thomas and the battle that changed American college sportIn the United States, swimmer Lia Thomas became one of the most prominent figures in the debate. Thomas competed for the University of Pennsylvania after transitioning and became the first openly transgender athlete to win an NCAA Division I individual title when she won the women's 500-yard freestyle in 2022.Her participation triggered intense debate over eligibility, fairness and the rules governing transgender athletes in collegiate sport.The issue has since moved well beyond one swimmer. In June 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled that laws in West Virginia and Idaho restricting transgender athletes from participating on female school and college teams did not violate Title IX. The court's decision cleared the way for states to maintain such restrictions based on biological sex.Emily Bridges and the battle over cyclingCycling produced another highly visible case through British rider Emily Bridges. Bridges, who had previously competed in men's cycling, sought to compete in women's events after transitioning. Her eligibility became the subject of intense debate in 2022 when she was ruled ineligible for the women's event at the British National Omnium Championships.The wider issue eventually contributed to a significant change in international cycling policy. The Union Cycliste Internationale, cycling's world governing body, changed its rules in 2023 and prohibited transgender women who transitioned after male puberty from competing in women's events on its international calendar. The organisation said its decision was based on the available scientific evidence and the need to protect equal opportunities in the women's category.Imane Khelif: The boxing controversy that blurred the linesThe transgender debate in sport is also frequently linked to another high-profile case, but Imane Khelif's story needs to be treated separately.Khelif is not a transgender athlete. The Algerian boxer was born and raised as a woman and competed in the women's 66kg category at the Paris 2024 Olympics, where she went on to win the gold medal.Yet her participation became one of the biggest controversies of the Games.The issue stemmed from a dispute between boxing's governing bodies. The International Boxing Association (IBA) said Khelif had failed its eligibility requirements at the 2023 World Championships and claimed that testing had found her ineligible to compete in the women's category. However, the IBA did not publicly release the underlying test results. The IOC, which was responsible for the boxing competition at Paris 2024, rejected the IBA's position and allowed Khelif to compete.The WNBA debate tooThe conversation has also reached women's basketball in the United States. Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham recently reignited the debate after speaking publicly about transgender participation in women's sport. Her comments generated both support and criticism, forcing the WNBA to address an issue that had largely remained outside the league's immediate competitive spotlight.WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert subsequently told teams that the league would continue discussing transgender participation, acknowledging the growing attention surrounding the issue.The situation is particularly interesting because there is currently no openly transgender player competing in the WNBA.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Leon Baptiste: Other British athletes convicted in connection with coach's sex assault of minor in Morocco
articles.summary: BBC Sport reveals that Will Sharman, Richard Sharman and Lamin Deen were also convicted in the case which led to Leon Baptiste's imprisonment.
articles.body:
Three British former athletes were convicted in Morocco as part of an investigation into the sexual assault of a minor by a sprinting coach, BBC Sport can reveal.

The prosecutions led to the imprisonment of Leon Baptiste, a UK Athletics coach and 2010 Commonwealth Games gold medallist for England in the 200m.

Baptiste was originally reported as missing in Morocco in some media articles published on 14 August, before a BBC Sport investigation revealed his conviction and jailing.

Now, court rulings seen by BBC Sport shed more light on other convictions relating to the same case.

Two-time Commonwealth silver medallist hurdler Will Sharman, his brother and ex-bobsleigh athlete Richard Sharman, and fellow former bobsleigh competitor Lamin Deen, who were all on holiday with Baptiste, were convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.

Also convicted of the same offence were acquaintances Ashley O'Leary Jones and David Tuck.

The group said via their lawyers that they were never arrested and were unaware of their convictions until informed of them by BBC Sport.

A spokesperson for all five men told BBC Sport: "William, Richard, Lamin, David and Ashley are shocked and distressed by the circumstances in which they have unexpectedly found themselves.

"They reject any suggestion that they knowingly engaged in unlawful or improper conduct. They left Morocco believing they had complied with all requirements placed upon them.

"At the time, they understood that they had paid an administrative fine equivalent to approximately £40 and that the matter had concluded."

BBC Sport understands that police raided a villa in Tamensourt on the outskirts of Marrakech after a girl contacted them claiming she had been brought to the property, had not been paid money she was promised in exchange for sex with Baptiste, and that she had been assaulted by a housekeeper after she was accused of stealing a watch.

Baptiste, 41, was subsequently convicted of sexual assault of a minor and given a 10-month prison sentence, which was subsequently reduced to eight months on appeal.

Court documents refer to the girl as being 16 years old and say she suffered "psychological trauma, sexual exploitation, physical assault and injury, and the violation of her human dignity".

Court records show that in June the five men were given suspended sentences of four months and fines of 500 dirhams (£40) each after being convicted of participating in the enticement of a minor.

All five men were acquitted of a separate charge of inciting a minor to engage in prostitution.

The Morocco presidency of the public ministry, which oversees prosecutions in the country, provided BBC Sport with the court judgement regarding the group, which reads: "The defendants were in the company of [Leon Baptiste] and were seated at the same table as the minor, alongside her.

"They thereby assisted him in deceiving the minor and persuading her to engage in sexual relations [with Baptiste]. This constitutes participation in the enticement of a minor.

"The court found them guilty on this count and decided to convict them for these acts."

The group had already left Morocco by the time the decision was handed down. Their convictions and sentences were upheld after an appeal hearing in July.

In a response provided by their lawyers to BBC Sport, the Sharman brothers, Deen, O’Leary Jones and Tuck say they visited the Montecristo nightclub based on a recommendation provided by their driver, and had no reason to believe it was anything other than a respectable establishment.

They say they were unaware of the girl's age and that some members of the group do not even recall seeing her in the nightclub. The villa they were staying in was vast and the interaction between the men and Mr Baptiste while inside the villa was limited.

They also say that they were not present in court on any occasion, that the court process was not in English and that it was not explained to them.

The spokesperson continued: "What has unfolded over recent months has been a distressing and incoherent saga.

"They did not properly understand the proceedings and were completely shocked on being told that they were the subject of a criminal conviction, when that is not how they understood it."

Companies House records and a biography on one of O'Leary Jones' social media profiles show he is a director of a company operating five children's care homes in Greater Manchester.

Tuck's social media biography indicates he is a military veteran, while a CV posted online lists experience coaching women's and children's football clubs including at Stoke City, Apollon Limassol in Cyprus, and Orlando Pride in the USA.

When asked by BBC Sport to comment on the convictions and the potential safeguarding issues raised, the UK Foreign Office, Home Office, and Department for Culture, Media, and Sport declined to provide a response.

Records also show that other people were convicted in relation to the case.

They include the housekeeper of the villa and two of its security guards, who were each given a two-month suspended prison sentence and a fine of 5,000 dirhams (£396).

The manager of the Montecristo nightclub where the group met the girl was sentenced to two months in jail.

A waiter at the Montecristo was also prosecuted, as was the owner of the agency which rents out the villa.

The girl - a Moroccan national - was awarded civil compensation of 60,000 dirhams (£4,784), to be paid jointly by all of those convicted, plus court costs.

Baptiste is currently serving his sentence in Al-Oudaya prison, and resigned from his position as a consultant coach via a message sent on his behalf to UK Athletics on 18 August citing unspecified ill-health.

Baptiste will be deported from Morocco once he is released from prison.

His case was able to move through the system quickly, with only weeks between his initial arrest and sentencing, because Morocco operates a system in which Baptiste swiftly appeared before a judge and not a jury.

At an appeal hearing in July, two months were taken off his sentence.

The sprinters coached by Baptiste were unaware of the reason for his abrupt lack of contact since telling them he would be absent from training "for a while" in May.

Will Sharman won silver medals in the 110m hurdles at the Commonwealth Games in 2010 and 2014, as well as at the 2014 European Championships, and has worked on the BBC gameshow Gladiators.

The 41-year-old was also featured on BBC Radio 4 as an accomplished pianist in 2015, and appeared as a panel guest on an episode of A Question of Sport in 2014.

His brother Richard, 44, formerly competed in elite-level bobsleigh competitions for Great Britain. On social media he describes himself as an industrial engineer running his own company, as well as a pilot and investor.

Lamin Deen, 45, is a former lance sergeant who served in the grenadier guards during conflicts in Northern Ireland, Bosnia and Kosovo, and competed in bobsleigh at the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi and the 2018 edition in Pyeongchang.

He worked as a pundit for TNT Sports during the 2026 Games in Milan-Cortina.

In some online reviews and social media posts, the Montecristo is referred to as a known meeting place for sex workers and potential clients.

The venue was closed by Moroccan authorities during the investigation and has not reopened since.

A statement referring to the case was posted on its social media channels on 15 May, saying: "Montecristo would like to provide clarification and reaffirm its commitment to the values that have always defined us.

"We are treating this matter with the utmost seriousness and are fully co-operating with the relevant authorities in a spirit of transparency and responsibility."

BBC Sport has contacted Montecristo for comment but received no reply.

On Saturday the Moroccan charity Touche Pas À Mon Enfant (Don't Touch My Child) released a statement criticising the sentence Baptiste was given.

"While fully respecting judicial independence and the decisions handed down by competent courts, we cannot hide our astonishment and deep concern regarding a sentence of such duration in a case involving the sexual assault of a minor - particularly given that the sentence was reduced on appeal," the statement reads.

"Sexual assaults committed against children are not ordinary offences - they can leave victims with profound and lasting physical and psychological trauma.

"In this context, we question the precise legal classification of the acts and the circumstances that led to the imposition of this sentence and its subsequent reduction on appeal."

In 2016 UNAIDS estimated that around 75,000 sex workers were operating in Morocco.

The children's rights organisation Humanium has called sex tourism "a thriving industry" in Morocco.

articles.title: Hockey World Cup: Belgium break Indian hearts in shootout as Harmanpreet’s side finishes eighth
articles.summary: Hockey News: India’s spirited fightback ended in heartbreak as Belgium prevailed in a tense penalty shootout after the two sides played out a thrilling 3-3 draw in.
articles.body: India’s spirited fightback ended in heartbreak as Belgium prevailed in a tense penalty shootout after the two sides played out a thrilling 3-3 draw in regulation time. India had made the brighter start and took the lead through Abhishek, whose sixth-minute field goal gave the hosts a 1-0 advantage. Belgium responded with sustained pressure, earning multiple penalty corners, but India’s defence held firm.The match changed dramatically in the second quarter. Roman Duvekot restored parity for Belgium with a close-range finish before Hugo Labouchere put them ahead with a powerful drag-flick from a penalty corner. Belgium went into half-time 2-1 up.India came out strongly after the break and levelled through captain Harmanpreet Singh, who converted a penalty corner with a superb drag-flick in the 31st minute. Belgium challenged the goal with a review, but the decision went India's way.The third quarter remained fiercely contested, with Belgium applying pressure and India creating opportunities of their own. Despite Belgium enjoying more possession, India held their shape to take the scores level at 2-2 into the final quarter.Belgium strike again, India refuse to give upBelgium regained the lead in the 47th minute when Nicolas de Kerpel fired home a field goal. The goal was referred for a possible obstruction, but the original decision was upheld and Belgium moved 3-2 ahead. India were dealt another blow when veteran Manpreet Singh took a stick to the face and left the field for medical attention.With time running out, India pulled their goalkeeper in favour of an additional outfield player and threw numbers forward in search of an equaliser. Their gamble paid off in dramatic fashion.Harmanpreet struck again in the 60th minute, finding the target to make it 3-3 and force a penalty shootout.Shootout drama ends India's hopesThe shootout began disastrously for India. Harmanpreet's first attempt was saved by Belgium goalkeeper Vincent Vanasch after the Indian captain appeared to stop while expecting a whistle. Belgium converted their opening attempt, while Vanasch then denied Sukhjeet Singh as well.India eventually found their rhythm. Shilanand Lakra opened India's account before Belgium restored their advantage. Dilpreet Singh then converted to bring the shootout level at 2-2.Belgium regained the lead through a penalty stroke after Mohith was penalised for a foul on Van Dessel, with Hendrickx converting. India stayed alive when Abhishek scored to make it 3-3.The decisive moment came when Duvekot found the target for Belgium. India took a referral in an attempt to overturn the decision, but the call stood.Belgium therefore won the shootout and ended India's brave fight after an extraordinary contest and they finish 8th in this World Cup.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Why is National Sports Day celebrated on August 29? The remarkable Major Dhyan Chand story behind India’s Olympic hockey gold hat-trick
articles.summary: Hockey News: He scored more than 400 goals, inspired India’s dominance of world hockey and was the central figure in the country’s first hat-trick of Olympic gold .
articles.body: He scored more than 400 goals, inspired India’s dominance of world hockey and was the central figure in the country’s first hat-trick of Olympic gold medals. Decades after his playing career ended, Major Dhyan Chand remains one of the most revered figures in Indian sporting history.His contribution is remembered every year on August 29, his birth anniversary, which is celebrated across India as National Sports Day.The day, established in 2012, is a tribute to the hockey great popularly known as the ‘Hockey Wizard’ and ‘The Magician’. It also serves as a reminder of the importance of sports, physical activity and fitness, while providing an occasion to celebrate the achievements of India’s leading sportspersons.But why was Dhyan Chand chosen as the inspiration behind National Sports Day, and who was the man whose extraordinary hockey career helped put India at the top of the sporting world?Why is National Sports Day celebrated on August 29?National Sports Day is observed on August 29 because it marks the birth anniversary of Dhyan Chand, who was born in Allahabad, now Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh, in 1905.The annual observance was established in 2012 to honour his contribution to Indian hockey and to highlight the broader importance of sports and fitness in everyday life.The occasion has traditionally also been associated with the presentation of India’s major sporting honours. Over the years, the country’s top sports awards have been presented by the President of India at a ceremony at Rashtrapati Bhavan around National Sports Day.The country’s highest sporting honour, the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award, also carries the hockey legend’s name. The award was previously known as the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna before being renamed.National Sports Day is also marked by sporting and fitness activities at schools, colleges and other institutions across the country. The idea is to encourage young people to participate in sports and understand the importance of maintaining an active and healthy lifestyle.The government’s Khelo India programme, which began in its present form in 2017-18, has become one of its major initiatives aimed at promoting sports among different age groups.In 2019, Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched the Fit India Movement on National Sports Day, further strengthening the focus on physical fitness and active lifestyles.Who was Major Dhyan Chand?Dhyan Chand was born Dhyan Singh on August 29, 1905. He later became one of the defining figures of Indian hockey during the sport’s golden era.His international career stretched from 1926 to 1948, and he represented India in 185 matches, scoring more than 400 goals according to the figures traditionally associated with his career.His journey into hockey, however, was not immediate. As a youngster, his initial interest was reportedly in wrestling. He took up hockey at around the age of 14 and eventually joined the British Indian Army, where his extraordinary talent began to emerge.His dedication to the sport became legendary. With much of his day occupied by regimental duties, he would practise hockey at night under the moonlight. The story is widely associated with how he came to be known as Dhyan Chand, with ‘Chand’ meaning moon in Hindi.His rise was rapid. After impressing in Army competitions, he earned his place in the Indian team for the 1928 Olympic Games in Amsterdam.There was little indication that his international career would eventually become synonymous with Indian hockey’s greatest period of dominance.Dhyan Chand and India’s Olympic gold hat-trickDhyan Chand was a key figure as India won three successive Olympic gold medals in hockey at the 1928, 1932 and 1936 Games.At the 1928 Olympics, he scored two goals in India’s 3-2 victory over the Netherlands in the final and finished as the tournament’s leading scorer with 14 goals.His extraordinary scoring continued at the 1932 Games in Los Angeles, where India successfully defended its Olympic title.But it was at the 1936 Berlin Olympics that one of the most famous chapters of his career unfolded.India defeated Germany 8-1 in the final to complete a third consecutive Olympic hockey triumph. Dhyan Chand played a starring role, scoring two goals in the final. A famous account of the match says he played barefoot during the second half, although the detail has become part of the mythology surrounding his career.For India, Dhyan Chand and the hockey team provided one of the defining sporting performances of the Games.The hockey wizard who scored more than 400 goalsDhyan Chand’s reputation was built not merely on his goal tally but on the extraordinary control and skill he displayed with the hockey stick.His stick work, passing ability, positioning and understanding of the game earned him the enduring descriptions of ‘Hockey Wizard’ and ‘The Magician’.His career continued until 1948, when he was 42 years old. By then, he had become one of the most celebrated hockey players in the world.There are several famous stories surrounding his ability. One oft-repeated tale claims that officials at a match had his stick inspected because they suspected there was something unusual about it after watching his extraordinary control of the ball.Whether anecdotal or embellished over the years, such stories reflect the almost mythical status Dhyan Chand acquired during his career.His influence extended beyond his own achievements. His success helped establish India as a dominant force in international hockey during the pre-Independence era and inspired generations of players.Why Dhyan Chand remains relevant on National Sports DayDhyan Chand’s legacy goes beyond his three Olympic gold medals and remarkable scoring record.His career is remembered as an example of discipline, dedication, skill and commitment to sport — qualities that National Sports Day seeks to promote among young Indians.He was also recognised by the Indian government for his contribution to hockey. In 1956, he was awarded the Padma Bhushan, the country's third-highest civilian honour at the time.Dhyan Chand retired from the Army as a Major in the Punjab Regiment in 1956. He continued to be associated with hockey after his playing career, including through coaching and mentoring.His birth anniversary therefore became an appropriate occasion for India to celebrate not only one of its greatest sporting icons but the wider role of sport in society.August 29: Celebrating sport beyond Dhyan ChandNational Sports Day today has a much broader significance than remembering one hockey player.It is an opportunity to recognise athletes who have brought glory to India, encourage children to take up sport and promote physical fitness across society.From schools and colleges organising competitions and fitness activities to the recognition of outstanding sportspersons, August 29 has become a day when India turns its attention to the value of sporting excellence.Yet at the heart of the occasion remains the story of a young man named Dhyan Singh, who practised hockey under the moon after completing his military duties and went on to become one of the greatest players the sport has ever produced.Nearly half a century after his death, his name continues to define India’s National Sports Day — a fitting tribute to the man who helped make Indian hockey synonymous with Olympic greatness.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Was away physically for those weeks, but present mentally: Sjoerd Marijne
articles.summary: Hockey News: KOLKATA: It was 2020 and the pandemic had just begun.Sjoerd Marijne, then the coach of the Indian women's hockey team, was in a cab en route to Bengal.
articles.body: KOLKATA: It was 2020 and the pandemic had just begun.Sjoerd Marijne, then the coach of the Indian women's hockey team, was in a cab en route to Bengaluru airport, from where he was supposed to fly back to the Netherlands to join his family. But midway through the ride, he changed his mind and returned to the city's Sports Authority of India centre.It was a difficult decision, but Marijne chose to stay. A year later, he led India to a historic fourth-place finish at the Tokyo Olympics.Six years on, Marijne found himself making a very different choice. When he returned to take charge of the Indian women's team for a second stint, he once again had to find a way to combine his commitment to the team with being there for his family. This time, with the World Cup approaching, he chose to spend a few weeks with his family before rejoining the team - a decision that had been agreed upon when he took up the job.But while Marijne was away from the team physically, he remained closely connected with its preparations. He followed every training session and practice match, stayed in touch with the players and conducted video meetings to ensure he remained on top of the process."I saw every training session and every practice match. I saw everything. So I wasn't there in person, but I was there," Marijne told TOI in an exclusive interview after India recorded their best World Cup finish in 52 years. "I had contact with the players and did video meetings with them, so I was on top of the process."Marijne also credited his support staff, as well as the team's strength and conditioning staff, for giving him the confidence that the team was in good hands. "I had very good assistants like Matias Villa. Tim White, who is doing the under-21s, was also there. So, I knew they were in good hands," he said. "There's a lot of leadership in the team and they knew that they had to do well and give the example, so that's why this was possible."When Marijne re-joined, he found the squad had continued along the same path. "It was all the same. For the girls, it also felt like I hadn't been away. So that is a positive thing," he said.The Dutchman also stressed that while he was away physically, he had never stepped away from his responsibilities as coach. "It wasn't that for a few weeks I wasn't there mentally. I was only not physically there," he said.For Marijne, the experience also highlighted the growing maturity within the group. The players were able to take responsibility, lean on the senior members and stay true to the team's structure and culture even with their coach away from the training ground."The players knew that I was overseeing everything," he said. "The main thing is that it looked like I was away. I was away physically, but for the players it didn't feel like I was away because I was still involved."Perhaps that was the biggest reassurance for Marijne - that the team had developed enough trust and leadership to keep moving in the same direction, even when he wasn't physically there.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Rumesh Pathirage raises bar again, Neeraj Chopra braces for another test
articles.summary: More sports News: NEW DELHI: Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage's sensational season has entered another gear, and for India's Olympic and world champion Neeraj Chopra, the road.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage's sensational season has entered another gear, and for India's Olympic and world champion Neeraj Chopra, the road to the Diamond League Final and Asian Games now comes with an unmistakable warning.The Sri Lankan javelin star produced a breathtaking 92.07m in Zurich on Thursday to underline why he has become the man to beat this season. It was his second throw beyond 92m in 2026, following his world-leading 92.62m national record in Rome in June.The Zurich effort also pushed Pathirage into rare company. He is only the fourth javelin thrower in history to cross the 92m mark twice, joining legendary names such as Jan Zelezny, Johannes Vetter and Aki Parviainen.Pathirage had to work his way into the competition in Zurich. He opened with 81.50m, improved to 88.23m in the second round and reached 89.90m in the third. After 84.91m in the fourth round and a foul in the fifth, he delivered the knockout blow in the last throw.Former world champion Anderson Peters came second with a season-best 86.93m, while Poland's Dawid Wegner took third with a personal-best 85.16m.The victory was another chapter in Pathirage's extraordinary 2026 campaign. The 23-year-old has now won 11 of his 12 competitions this year, including his last six. After his Rome explosion, he won in Ostrava and at the Doha Diamond League before creating history in Glasgow as Sri Lanka's first Commonwealth Games javelin champion.He then edged out Chopra at the Lausanne Diamond League, winning with 88.14m, just nine centimetres better than the Indian's 88.05m. That was Chopra's best effort of the season.Chopra, a two-time Olympic medallist, skipped Zurich but still qualified for the Diamond League Final in Brussels as the sixth-ranked thrower. The season-ending showdown on Sept 4-5 now presents another major Pathirage-Chopra clash.And this is a rivalry that could carry even greater weight soon. After Brussels, both stars are set to have the Asian Games on their radar.For Chopra, the challenge is clear: Pathirage is no longer merely a rising contender. With consistency, distance and an extraordinary winning streak behind him, the Sri Lankan has transformed himself into the benchmark.Zurich only strengthened that message and the pressure, increasingly, is on Chopra. Pathirage's emergence has changed the javelin throw landscape, making every meeting with the Indian a potential season-defining contest ahead for both.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Kerr, tajante: "He competido contra tramposos dopados. El atletismo está plagado de ello"
articles.standfirst: En una entrevista en 'The Times', el atleta aseguró sobre Ingebrigtsen que "hace tiempo que no compito contra él, pero tenemos personalidades muy parecidas"
articles.summary: En una entrevista en 'The Times', el atleta aseguró sobre Ingebrigtsen que "hace tiempo que no compito contra él, pero tenemos personalidades muy parecidas"
articles.body: El británico Josh Kerr, que este año batió el récord mundial de la milla que tenía El Guerrouj, aseguró que "he competido contra tramposos dopados. El atletismo está plagado de ello". En una entrevista en 'The Times', el atleta explicó que "competí en la primera ronda de 1500 metros del Mundial de Londres en 2017 contra atletas que posteriormente fueron descalificados por dopaje. Nuestro deporte está lleno de ello". Así, el británico explicó que "si hubiera hecho trampa, mi mentalidad se vería afectada porque lo sabría. Pero si sé que he hecho todo bien, desde el entrenamiento hasta la nutrición, el sueño y la hidratación, entonces mi mente está en paz. Incluso puedo perder una carrera y aun así sentir que lo di todo. Hacer las cosas bien me hace más fuerte. Y saber que mis rivales buscan atajos me hace aún más rápido". Sobre su rivalidad con Jakob Ingebrigtsen, que criticó recientemente la ausencia de Kerr en el Europeo de Birmingham, Kerr hizo hincapié en que "hace tiempo que no compito contra él, pero tenemos personalidades muy parecidas, así que, en cuanto a competitividad, seguro que chocamos. Sé que él no se va a callar, y yo tampoco. Pero eso atrae al público y da lugar a carreras fantásticas, y estoy orgulloso de ello". Pero Josh, que se verá las caras con el noruego en un duelo en 1.500 en el Ultimate de Budapest, insistió en que "ahora mismo, sin embargo, estoy centrado en mí. Estoy centrado en ser recordado como el mejor corredor de la milla de todos los tiempos”.

articles.title: Neeraj Chopra’s 2026 season over after ankle ligament tear, Diamond League Final and Asian Games ruled out
articles.summary: More sports News: NEW DELHI: India’s javelin star Neeraj Chopra’s 2026 season has come to a premature end after the Olympic and world champion suffered a ligament tear .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India’s javelin star Neeraj Chopra’s 2026 season has come to a premature end after the Olympic and world champion suffered a ligament tear in his ankle during training, ruling him out of next month’s Diamond League Final and Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.Chopra made the announcement on Saturday, revealing that the injury occurred shortly after he produced a season’s best throw at the Lausanne Diamond League. Following consultations with his doctor and support team, the 28-year-old decided against taking any further competitive risk and will now focus on rehabilitation.The setback comes at a particularly frustrating juncture for Chopra, who had begun to feel that he was finally rediscovering the consistency and momentum he had been searching for this season.“After a period of hard work, I finally felt I was gaining the momentum I had been looking for with a Season’s Best throw in Lausanne,” Chopra said in a statement. “Unfortunately, shortly after, I sustained a ligament tear in my ankle during training. After discussions with my doctor and team, we’ve decided that I will sit out the rest of this season.“It’s disappointing, especially because I felt close to finding my rhythm. But as they say, setbacks are a part of the journey.“My focus now is on recovering well and coming back even stronger.”The injury means Chopra will miss the Asian Games, where he was expected to spearhead India’s medal campaign in athletics. His absence will be a major setback for the country’s hopes at the continental showpiece, which begins next month in Japan.Chopra’s 2026 campaign had been a mixed one. He returned to competition at the Doha Diamond League in June following a lengthy injury layoff and finished fourth with a throw of 85.69m. He then won silver in Glasgow with an 85.83m effort, although Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Pathirage stole the spotlight by clinching gold with a huge 89.75m throw.The Lausanne Diamond League was Chopra’s third competitive appearance of the season and had offered signs that he was moving closer to his best. His season’s-best effort there had provided a much-needed confidence boost and was expected to serve as an important build-up to the Asian Games.Instead, Lausanne has turned out to be his final competition of the year.Chopra will also miss the Diamond League Final. He had moved up to seventh in the qualification standings and remained in contention for a place in the season-ending event, but the ankle injury has now brought his campaign to a halt.For Chopra, the priority is now clear: recover fully, avoid rushing his comeback and return to competition at full strength.For India, however, his absence leaves a significant void heading into the Asian Games, where the defending Olympic champion was expected to be one of the country’s biggest medal hopes.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Neeraj Chopra’s injury battles: From elbow surgery in 2019 to an ankle ligament tear in 2026 - the setbacks and comebacks that defined his career
articles.summary: More sports News: Neeraj Chopra’s career has been defined by historic throws, Olympic medals and a relentless pursuit of excellence. But alongside those milestones has .
articles.body: Neeraj Chopra’s career has been defined by historic throws, Olympic medals and a relentless pursuit of excellence. But alongside those milestones has been a recurring challenge: injuries that have repeatedly interrupted his season.Neeraj Chopra has been ruled out of the 2026 Asian Games and the remainder of the season after suffering an ankle ligament tear during training. The injury comes just days after he finished second at the Lausanne Diamond League with a season-best 88.05m. It is another frustrating setback for the two-time Olympic medallist, who had only recently returned from a lengthy injury layoff.Here is a look at the major injury setbacks that have disrupted his career.2026: An ankle tear ends his seasonChopra's latest injury is an ankle ligament tear sustained during training. The injury rules him out of the Asian Games, the Diamond League Final and the World Athletics Ultimate Championships, bringing his 2026 campaign to an early end.It comes after a promising return to competition following almost nine months away from the sport.2025-26: A long road back from a back injuryChopra's previous major setback came with a back injury that kept him away from competition for around nine months. He had competed at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo despite carrying the problem, finishing eighth. The injury subsequently forced him into an extended rehabilitation period.His comeback was delayed further in 2026, with Chopra missing the Doha Diamond League before eventually returning to competitive action.2024: Adductor concerns before ParisThe 2024 season brought another fitness scare. Chopra withdrew from the Ostrava Golden Spike after experiencing discomfort in his adductor. Chopra subsequently opted out of the Paris Diamond League, again because of his troublesome adductor/groin issue. He later explained that he did not want to take unnecessary risks with the Paris Olympics approaching.The decision paid off as Chopra stayed fit for the Olympics and successfully defended his place on the podium, winning silver in Paris.2023: Three meets on the sidelinesIn 2023, a muscle strain forced Chopra to miss three competitions in quick succession - the FBK Games, Paavo Nurmi Games and Ostrava Golden Spike. He missed roughly a month of competition before returning at the Lausanne Diamond League.2022: Groin injury costs him Commonwealth GamesAfter winning his first World Championships medal in Eugene, Chopra suffered a groin injury that ruled him out of the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham. It was a major disappointment for the Indian star, who was the defending champion after winning gold at the 2018 Commonwealth Games.2019: The first major interruptionOne of the earliest and most significant injury setbacks of Chopra's career came in 2019. A right elbow injury required surgery and forced him to miss the World Championships that year. It also kept him away from competition for several months. articles.title: 'We need to be stronger defensively': Harmanpreet  after India’s eighth-place in Hockey World Cup
articles.summary: Hockey News: India captain Harmanpreet Singh admitted that the team needs to strengthen its defence after the men's side ended a disappointing Hockey World Cup cam.
articles.body: India captain Harmanpreet Singh admitted that the team needs to strengthen its defence after the men's side ended a disappointing Hockey World Cup campaign in eighth place. India's hopes of avoiding the eighth-place finish were dashed by co-hosts Belgium, who edged them 4-3 in a penalty shootout after the two teams played out a 3-3 draw in regulation time.Belgium led 3-2 until the closing stages, but Harmanpreet converted a penalty corner with just 26 seconds remaining to force the match into a shootout. The Indian skipper finished the tournament with eight goals.‘Not happy with eighth-place finish’Harmanpreet acknowledged that India took confidence from their performance against one of the world's leading teams but admitted the final position was disappointing.“Playing against the world's top team in front of their fans and performing well as a team is a big boost. We're happy with the performance against Belgium, but not with the eighth-place finish,” he said.India had started the tournament strongly, beating Wales 3-1 and Pakistan 5-3 before losing 2-4 to England in the pool stage. Their campaign then unravelled in the second round, with defeats against the Netherlands and Argentina ending their hopes of reaching the semi-finals.Defence remains a concernHarmanpreet said the tournament had highlighted the need for India to improve collectively in defence, particularly against the world's top teams.“If we don't defend well as a team, big teams will trouble you. We need to be stronger defensively. This is one area where we lagged behind,” the captain said.“There are no individual goals. If we win, we win as a team, and if we lose, it is also collective responsibility,” he added.Asian Games now the targetDespite the disappointing World Cup campaign, Harmanpreet said India must quickly shift their focus to their next major objective - the Asian Games.“This is a journey, and now our next goal is the Asian Games. We want to win the gold medal there and qualify for the Los Angeles Olympics,” he said.Harmanpreet's eight goals were one of the few bright spots from India's campaign, but the eighth-place finish means the team will now have to address its defensive shortcomings as it begins the road towards the Asian Games and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Women’s Hockey World Cup: Argentina stun Netherlands in shootout thriller to win third title
articles.summary: Hockey News: Argentina women’s hockey team achieved a miracle on Saturday as they beat world No. 1 and three-time defending champions Netherlands in the World Cup .
articles.body: Argentina women’s hockey team achieved a miracle on Saturday as they beat world No. 1 and three-time defending champions Netherlands in the World Cup final at Wagener Stadium in Amstelveen to lift the title for the third time.Playing in front of a raucous crowd, the South Americans were crowned world champions after winning 3-1 in a shoot-out, following a 1-1 draw at the end of 60 minutes. Goalkeeper Cristina Cosentino was the star, producing a string of superb saves — during the shoot-out as well as in regulation time — to help Argentina pull off the upset.Cosentino was duly named Player of the Match and, speaking after the game, could not have been prouder of her teammates and what they had achieved.After all, this was the first time since 2010 that the Dutch women lost a World Cup final. And 16 years ago, it was Argentina who had beaten them to claim the title for the second time — their first coming in 2002, also by defeating Netherlands.On Saturday, however, it seemed for a long time that Argentina would not be able to repeat that feat. They had lost the 2022 final too, and it looked like history was going to repeat itself as Netherlands took the lead in the 30th minute through Yibbi Jansen from a penalty corner and continued to hold on to their advantage well into the final quarter.But Argentina simply refused to give up.They kept pushing the Dutch back and won numerous PCs. The Dutch defence held firm for much of the contest, but eventually Argentina found a way through in the 54th minute.Following their seventh penalty corner, a mistrap saw Agustina Gorzelany fire the ball towards goal. A Dutch defender managed to get a stick to it, but the ball fell to Maria Granatto, who made no mistake from the left of the D, finding the back of the net to bring Argentina level with six minutes remaining.The equaliser appeared to shake the Dutch, who completely lost their composure in the shoot-out.Pien Sanders, Felice Albers and Freeke Moes all failed to convert their attempts as Cosentino produced a sensational performance in goal. For Argentina, Zoe Diaz’s effort was ruled out for backstick, but Victoria Granatto, Brisa Bruggesser and Sofia Cairo all found the net to seal a 3-1 victory.Earlier, the final was a cagey affair, with neither side creating too many clear-cut opportunities. Late in the first quarter, Pien Dicke had a couple of chances, but Cosentino stood firm to keep the Dutch at bay.Jansen eventually gave the Dutch the lead late in the second quarter, but they were unable to impose the kind of control they are renowned for.Argentina, meanwhile, kept believing and pushing until they finally found a way back into the contest. And when the shoot-out arrived, Cosentino produced the defining moments to help Argentina complete a stunning victory and lift their third World Cup title.Meanwhile, in the other match of the day, Belgium beat Australia 1-0 to finish in third place.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
