articles.title: 2026 Sydney Marathon: Addisu Gobena sets men's course record in victory; Peres Jepchirchir wins women's race
articles.summary: Gobena finished second in Sydney a year ago. He came out on top this time around.
articles.body:
A runner-up last year in the Sydney Marathon, Ethiopian Addisu Gobena won the event on Saturday, emerging from a field that featured the 2025 winner, fellow Ethiopian Hailemaryam Kiros, and the reigning world champion, Tanzania's Alphonce Simbu.

Gobena, 21, smashed Kiros' course record of 2:06:06 with a time of 2:04:42.

Although Simbu was taken down, the 2025 world champion on the women's side, Kenya's Peres Jepchirchir, wasn't defeated in Australia. The 32-year-old Jepchirchir, a 2021 Olympic gold medalist, finished just nine seconds shy of the course record, clocking in at 2:18:31.

In its second year as a World Marathon major — there are currently seven (the others are Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago and New York City) — the Sydney Marathon hosted around 40,000 expected runners who raced from North Sydney, across the Sydney Harbor Bridge and to the finish line, which was located in front of the city's iconic Opera House.

The Sydney Marathon marked the fourth event on this year's Marathon Major calendar. With a more demanding course than some of the majors, there was once again plenty of intrigue in Sydney. Last year, Kiros finished first among the men, while Sifan Hassan, a three-time Olympic gold medalist representing the Netherlands, took home the women's in 2:18:22. She didn't take part in Saturday's race, however.

This time around, Kenya's Priscah Cherono led all women at the 10-kilometer mark. The 46-year-old, who won the Los Angeles Marathon earlier this year after recently making a comeback from a five-year hiatus , was being chased by a collection of elites. That group included Jepchirchir, her compatriot.

Cherono was finally caught, about 30 kilometers in. Jepchirchir surged and so did Tanzania's Magdalena Shauri and Kenya's Irine Cheptai. Jepchirchir and Cheptai ultimately overtook Cherono, and Jepchirchir pulled ahead near the 35-kilometer mark.

In the end, no one reeled in Jepchirchir, who was stunningly close to topping Hassan's course record from a year ago.

As for the men's race, through 20 kilometers, it was on pace to shatter the course record. Humorously, two people dressed as Mario and Luigi were matching the speed of the lead runners for a good bit of time while on the sidelines.

Notably, Ethiopian Sisay Lemma dropped back from the top group as the race wore on. Lemma won Boston in 2024 but has struggled with injuries in recent years.

Through 40 kilometers, the men's pack was seven deep, with Kiros, Gobena and Simbu all contending.

Gobena made his move and wound up taking more than a minute off the previous course record Kiros had notched, holding off another Ethiopian, Chimdessa Debele, with a final push.

articles.title: ‘We have to do it over and over’: Sjoerd Marijne on India’s next challenge
articles.summary: Hockey News: Kolkata: India’s best World Cup finish in 52 years has given the women’s hockey team a significant boost in confidence, but coach Sjoerd Marijne belie.
articles.body: Kolkata: India’s best World Cup finish in 52 years has given the women’s hockey team a significant boost in confidence, but coach Sjoerd Marijne believes the real challenge is to sustain that level. In an exclusive conversation with TOI, the Dutchman reflected on India’s campaign, the team’s growing discipline and belief, and the challenges ahead at the Asian Games. Excerpts...What do you think helped this team compete so consistently?I think the discipline, the structure, the talent, the belief and working as a unit made the difference.Since you took over the team, what changes have you seen in the players?From the beginning until now, I have seen them enjoying themselves more. They are having fun with each other, they are bonding and they understand the culture and what we want to achieve.What do you think this World Cup has changed in the team?The most important thing is that we believe more in ourselves and we have proven that we can achieve at a high level. It’s not just about saying we can do it, we actually did it.Do you feel we have now taken a step towards becoming a top-level side?We did really well in the tournament, but it doesn’t say anything about the future. The fact that we now beat Germany doesn’t mean we are always going to beat them. The girls have seen that we can do it. I don’t have to tell them anymore because we have proven we can do it. But now we have to do it over and over.What will be the biggest challenge in the Asian Games?I know the expectations are higher now. After the World Cup, everybody now expects more and so do the girls themselves. That’s fine. But we also have to learn to deal with that and we have to focus on ourselves.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
